scope: Bounded follow-up on the strongest island and aggregate local-food records: Rapa Nui, Tikopia, and Cahokia/American Bottom.

review_summary.disposition: Rapa Nui is an unusually strong exact-island validation case, and Tikopia has unusually explicit calorie, protein, land-area and rotation accounting. Neither can train the 1337 global scale: Rapa Nui has no independently measured saturation fraction and is an out-of-period analogue; Tikopia is unmapped in EU5 and post-period. Cahokia remains a city/trade-hub and flood-shock case rather than a rural capacity target.

records.label: Rapa Nui resilient pre-contact food system
records.population_interval_status: contact-era low-thousands estimate plus recent archaeological/genetic bounds; not a dated 1337 census
records.capacity_interval_status: two food-model regimes (low bioavailable nitrogen approximately 3,500; high nitrogen approximately 17,500), not an observed saturation interval

local_food_evidence.food_regime: sweet-potato and lithic-mulch horticulture, coastal groundwater, marine foods and local wild foods

pressure_evidence: The island is only 164 km2 and all food and freshwater constraints are geographically local.

DiNapoli et al. fit four demographic models to 201 radiocarbon dates from 47 residential/subsistence deposits; all show steady growth and no pre-contact collapse (Nature Communications 12, 3939, Results/Table 1 and Fig. 3).

The same paper reports that the low-N 3,500-person food-limited scenario is most consistent with the low-thousands contact estimate, while explicitly treating the 17,500 high-N result as assumption-dependent.
Lima et al. 2024 island-wide SWIR analysis substantially reduces the area of rock gardens and argues against using a 17,000-person population as an automatic capacity label.
rejection_reasons: The 3,500/17,500 alternatives are outputs of a food-budget model, not independent historical upper and lower observations; a model-versus-model interval would leak assumptions into training.
The ABC study supports resilience and no observed collapse, but does not establish what fraction of intrinsic 1337 capacity the population occupied. Lack of collapse is not proof of saturation.
The date extends to European contact in 1722 and the strongest direct population evidence is post-1337; fixed policy therefore restricts this record to held-out validation.
Exact semantic mapping is available and calibrated area is 164 km2 (matching the published island area), so this is a high-value validation fixture even though it is not a training anchor.
citation_locators: DiNapoli et al. 2021, Nature Communications 12:3939, abstract and Fig. 1 (164 km2 island), Results/Table 1/Fig. 3 (four logistic models), Discussion paragraphs on the 3,500 versus 17,500 food-limited scenarios.
DiNapoli et al. 2021, Methods: 201 radiocarbon determinations from 47 residential or subsistence locations.
Lima et al. 2024, Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.ado1459, island-wide SWIR rock-garden area and revised population-support range.
records.notes: Use as an exact-island monotonicity, uncertainty and small-area benchmark. Do not fit the global scale or turn model capacity into a target.

records.label: Tikopia stable 1929 system and 1952 population-pressure case
records.population_interval_status: enumerated 1929 and 1952 populations; 1952 includes documented hurricane and pressure effects
records.capacity_interval_status: multi-formula land/food ceiling: 1929 near maximum; 1,753 exceeds stable agricultural capacity; not a 1337 observation

local_food_evidence.food_regime: taro, yam, manioc, breadfruit, bananas, coconuts, fish and wild fruits

pressure_evidence: Hervad-Jorgensen measured 4.42 km2 total island area and 3.90 km2 cultivable area; 0.27 ha per person including fallow and 0.075 ha per person per year of active production.

The 1929 population was 1,278 and was described as a stable agricultural system; independent Conklin, Gourou, Beguin and Carneiro checks converge on being near the possible maximum (pp. 92-94, especially the conclusion on p. 95).

The 1952 population of 1,753 required a three-year rotation, caused severe resource pressure, and required approximately 475 ha to feed at the earlier standard—more than the island's 442 ha (pp. 93-95).
The article separates calorie and high-quality protein accounting and reports a 1929 diet of roughly 2,260 kcal/person/day and 31 g high-quality protein/person/day (p. 90, Table 1).
rejection_reasons: This is post-1337 ethnographic/modern evidence and therefore validation-only under the fixed analogue policy.
No Tikopia location tag or polygon exists in the current 20,929-location EU5 geometry inventory, so the exact island boundary cannot yet be scored.

The 1,100-1,400 capacity interval is a reconstruction from the same 1929/1952 food-area accounting, not an independent historical target; retain it as a diagnostic until a separate population/pressure source and EU5 crosswalk are available.
records.boundary_status: exact historical island boundary, currently unmapped

candidate_crosswalk.required_action: add or verify a Tikopia island polygon/tag, then compare calibrated area to 4.42 km2

citation_locators: Hervad-Jorgensen 1977, Geografisk Tidsskrift 76, pp. 90-91: energy/protein requirements, local diet and fish contribution.
Hervad-Jorgensen 1977, pp. 91-92: 442 ha total, 390 ha cultivable, 345 ha needed for 1,278 people, and rotation requirements.
Hervad-Jorgensen 1977, pp. 93-95: Conklin/Gourou/Beguin/Carneiro checks, 1929 near maximum, 1,753 too numerous for a stable system, and approximately 475 ha needed in 1952.
Firth, Borrie and Spillius 1957, Population Studies 10(3): enumerated population and demographic-pressure context.
records.notes: This is the strongest explicit local-food pressure/area benchmark found in this pass, but its lack of EU5 mapping and out-of-period date block training.

records.label: Cahokia/American Bottom floodplain population and food-pressure sequence
records.population_interval_status: urban-core and broad regional archaeological estimates with incompatible boundaries

local_food_evidence.food_regime: maize, beans, squash, floodplain fish/waterfowl and managed woodland foods

pressure_evidence: Munoz et al. identify a major Mississippi flood around AD 1200 that could inundate croplands, food caches and settlements, followed by relocation and decline by AD 1350 (PNAS 2015, Figs. 2-4).
Fecal-stanol and sediment-core work compares regional population proxies with flood and precipitation series, but explicitly leaves political and urban reorganization as confounders.
The American Bottom was a mixed urban, rural, wetland and upland system with exchange; local maize and floodplain foods do not prove intrinsic local equilibrium for the urban population.
rejection_reasons: Cahokia's strongest numerical estimate is an urban core or a broad polity total; the core is a trade/political hub and cannot supervise surrounding land capacity.

The existing EU5 cahokia location tag is a city-cell proxy, while the American Bottom research boundary is a heterogeneous regional floodplain. Substituting the city cell or whole cahokia province would violate the boundary contract.
Flood and drought are strong physical stress evidence but do not establish a two-sided Malthusian saturation fraction, and the AD 1200-1350 collapse sequence includes relocation and political shocks.
records.boundary_status: city tag exists but rural American Bottom boundary unresolved

candidate_crosswalk.boundary_confidence: high for historical description; zero for EU5 aggregate mapping
candidate_crosswalk.required_action: reconstruct a non-urban American Bottom research polygon before any quantitative scoring

citation_locators: Munoz et al. 2015, PNAS 112(20):6185-6190, Figs. 2-4 and discussion of the AD 1200 flood and AD 1350 dissolution.
White et al. 2019, PNAS, fecal stanols and sediment cores from Horseshoe Lake (Methods/Figs. 1-4), with explicit population-proxy and hydroclimate comparison.
Illinois State Archaeological Survey Cahokia synthesis: distinction between roughly 20,000 urban-core estimate and larger regional population.
records.notes: Retain as a held-out floodplain/urban-versus-rural diagnostic. No city estimate is used as a capacity label.
